title: micro-practices as portals to your art
content:
on making your art feel more accessible to yourself

in a recent post, threading your art into your day, I wrote about how I’ve been shifting my relationship to my creative practices from daily rituals/sprints that I felt pressured to make consistent time for (and then would very guilty when I didn’t/couldn’t)… into, instead, a shimmering thread that I’d then gently interweave into the fabric of my day.

this has meant reframing the work that is precious to me — writing, drawing, imaginative watery time — from a boundaried fragile thing that I had “protect at all costs” — like building castle walls to prevent enemy encroachment — into a tangible, flexible substance that I could touch, feel, pick up, and hold throughout the day. this means that my creative practice is no longer a precious thing I must protect, but a precious thing which protects me. it grounds me, nourishes me, and is always available to remind me of who I really am.

what’s helped me a lot in this transition is moving from digital to analog forms. the tactility matters a lot in making it feel real and immediate. and therefore, more accessible. it’s there. I just have to open the notebook cover.

this is the whole point of rituals, isn’t it? to make creative practices feel more accessible. to shorten the distance between the cluttered world of external life and worldly disasters — and to soften the arrival into the inner place, the eye of the storm, where we’re reminded of why we’re alive and here in the first place.

this is a very long introduction to say…

working with micro-practices

today, I want to share a concept that’s helped me tremendously in this shift. I call it micro-practices — 3 minutes, 7 minutes, 12 minutes — as tiny, almost negligible containers of time that allows me a way into my creative practices while sideskirting the resistance coming from my brain that might say… no no no, but we’re too busy/tired/distracted/in the wrong headspace for this right now…

tiny containers of time

the exact number you choose to work with is completely up to you, but I’ve conceptualized it as such…

3-5 minutes — truly micro, but most songs fit this length
6-8 minutes — tiny, but substantive enough to boil an egg
12-15 minutes — a serious chapter of time, enough to be transported
25 minutes — no longer a true micro-practice, more like a tomato-based workout

when I think micro-practice, I imagine sake-glass sized containers of time. time is an elastic, relative thing anyway, so allowing ourselves tiny glasses means that we can drink more of our creative practice, anytime.

and — we human beings regularly spend 3, 7, 12 minutes waiting in line at the grocery store or post office, listening to staticky elevator music on hold with customer service, scrolling to toxic media, waiting in traffic for the light to change, writing an email, examining a pimple, or, antagonizing over the little decisions that don’t, ultimately, make a difference in our lives.

we can afford 3, 7, 12 minutes to tend to a little creative seed in our souls, to write a few lines in a notebook, sketch something, or, doodle an idea. ultimately, the more you do it, it no longer feels like something to “afford,” but a cherished gift to yourself. then maybe, as essential as water.

micro-practices as entryways

micro-practices isn’t the same as a daily ritual. there’s no set time where you have to do them. it’s not so much about building a robust habit that you execute when prompted, like a computer, but about giving yourself consistent 24/7 access to a slippery slide, into the pool of your own creativity.

here’s how I work with micro-practices (these days):

  1. I reach for my physical container (a notebook + pen/pencil of some kind)

  2. I set a 3-7-12 minute timer, maybe play a song.

  3. I take 10 seconds to sense into my body. I start the timer.

  4. when I finish, I log it somewhere in my notebook (with a dot, or a flower icon) to allow myself to look back and feel satisfied.

  5. I repeat again later.


remember that the micro-practice is just the way in. and sometimes, this is more than enough. the momentum of the tidal waves might carry you in deeper. or, after 7 minutes, you’ll feel like you’ve touched something tender or essential and nourishing, and you feel completely satiated for now. the point is that you emerge from these micro-practices knowing and trusting — in an embodied, deep way — that your creative practices are always there, waiting for you to arrive.
author: Kening Zhu
